name: Sharpen an outdoor knife properly
blurb: A knife that shaves is a safer knife. The skill is holding one consistent angle for the length of the stroke, and knowing when the burr tells you to switch sides.
gear: A coarse and a fine sharpening stone, diamond or ceramic
A strop, or a leather belt with polishing compound
steps: Determine the existing bevel angle — most outdoor knives sit around 20 degrees per side — and commit to matching it.
Work the coarse stone in consistent strokes until you can feel a burr along the whole length of the opposite edge. The burr is the only reliable signal that you have reached the apex.
Flip and repeat until the burr forms on the other side.
Move to the fine stone with lighter pressure and alternate sides to minimise the burr.
Strop on leather, edge trailing, to remove the last of the burr and polish the apex.
Test on paper, then on arm hair, then on wood — and touch up little and often rather than waiting for blunt.
tips: Inconsistent angle is the only real beginner problem. An angle guide or a marker pen on the bevel makes errors visible.
More pressure does not mean faster. It rounds the apex and ruins the edge.
proof: A dull knife, sharpened by you, cleanly slices a hanging sheet of paper and shaves arm hair.
